headline: Investment bonds and company structures becoming more attractive alternatives to super amid CGT reforms, Division 296 and proposed 30% minimum trust tax
reasoning: Liam Shorte argues that recent budget changes affecting Division 296 and trust taxation have made investment bonds — previously considered old-fashioned — increasingly attractive. These bonds are taxed internally at up to 30%, with some bond fund managers achieving effective rates of 12–17%. After a 10-year lock-up, earnings can be withdrawn tax-free. A simple investment company structure funded via a loan (rather than equity) is another option, allowing drawdowns of the loan without dividend tax complications, though accessing growth and income requires waiting until a lower tax bracket is achievable. He frames both as complements to super rather than replacements.
quote: The change in the budget's really just affected all the planning that people had done about Division 296 or about where young people who wanted to retire before 60 would invest. And suddenly these old style products, investment bonds, which have been judged up over the last decade, they're suddenly becoming more attractive. You're basically locking money away for 10 years, but after that 10 years, you can take the earnings out without paying any further tax. They're taxed internally at a maximum of 30%. So in some cases, some of these bond fund managers are able to get the tax rate down between 12 and 17%. So it is very attractive as an alternative or a we call it a compliment to super and certainly for those on high incomes, it's a way of saving for that early part of retirement without paying huge personal income tax on the investments.

headline: Australian trust law and tax legislation riddled with holes — Division 296 flip-flopping, testamentary trust backflips, and an inadequate discretionary-to-fixed trust election mechanism that punishes mistakes permanently with no exemptions for death, divorce, fraud or elder abuse
reasoning: Liam Shorte criticises the government's pattern of rushing out tax and superannuation legislation and then patching holes after the fact. He highlights Division 296 as an example of unrealised gains being added and removed, and indexation being toggled. The latest trust law changes initially included testamentary trusts then excluded them. The proposed fix — an election to convert discretionary trusts into fixed trusts to avoid state stamp duty on restructuring — is described as totally inadequate and potentially worse than the problem it solves. Most critically, if a trustee makes a distribution that deviates from the fixed election, the CGT exemption is lost permanently with no carve-outs for death, divorce, fraud, elder abuse or loss of capacity. Shorte labels this year's output 'Swiss cheese legislation' and expects industry associations to return to Treasury with a long list of missed issues.
quote: Look, I'm tired of, you know, the government rushing out changes in legislation and then having to fix holes in it. You know, we, we saw this with the Division 296, you know, unrealized gains in unrealized gains out indexation in indexation out. You know, it's now we're seeing with the, these changes to trust law, first the, the testamentary trusts were going to be included in these changes. Now they're, they're not. And then they've brought in this election to basically turn the trust from a discretionary trust basically into a fixed trust to try and avoid the problems with any restructuring causing stamp duty and other taxes with, with the states. But you know, the, the first initial look at their, at their fix is that it's, it's totally inadequate. And it's probably going to mean that even more people may get hit with stamp state stamp duty if they do any changes in the restructuring. So, yeah, and and you know, it's really draconian. You do you take this election to do fixed distributions for the future. And if you make, if you make a mistake or you make a, a the wrong distribution, not in line with those, you lose the exemption for, for life. There's no going back. So it's a you, you can't fix it. But that means that something like a death, a divorce, someone that had been subject to fraud, elder abuse, loss of capacity, all of those things would you would usually think would be built into the legislation as exemptions if something, you know, happened. None of that's been mentioned. So again, we're going to probably see all the associations going back to the Treasury and going you miss this, this and this, get your acting gear. So I'm calling this year's taxes and legislation the Swiss cheese legislation because they're full of holes.

headline: Retirees risk breaching contribution caps by moving to pension phase too quickly after year-end contributions, especially with Payday Super changes
reasoning: Liam Shorte warns that retirees who maximise concessional contributions near year-end and then immediately roll over to pension phase or transfer to a new fund risk breaching their caps if their employer makes an additional contribution. With Payday Super requiring more frequent super payments, the risk of an unexpected employer contribution is heightened. Once a rollover or transition to pension phase occurs, it is too late to amend the notice of intent to claim a tax deduction. His advice is to wait a couple of days after year-end before claiming the tax deduction and then moving to pension phase.
quote: Some people put extra contributions in to maximise their contributions, but hadn't checked that whether their employer was putting in another contribution, especially with Payday Super coming up, where super had to be paid weekly from now on. Well, unfortunately, it's too late once you've rolled over or you've moved into pension phase. It's too late to go back and change your notice of intent to claim. So it's a lesson learned for people. Don't try and push things too far. Leave it a couple of days after the end of the year to claim your tax deduction, and then you can move into the pension phase.
